text: What are the two main troubleshooting approaches?

options.text: Top-Down and Bottom-Up
Linear and Half-Split
Sequential and Random
Fast and Slow

explanation: The two main approaches are Linear (step by step from one end to the other) and Half-Split (test the midpoint first, then narrow down).

text: How does the Linear troubleshooting approach work?

options.text: Test the midpoint of the system first, then split the remaining half
Work through the system from one end to the other, checking each component in sequence
Replace all components simultaneously to find the fault quickly
Start at the most likely fault point and work outwards

explanation: The Linear approach works through the system from one end to the other, checking each component or stage in sequence until the fault is found.

text: How does the Half-Split troubleshooting approach work?

options.text: Check every component one by one from start to finish
Split the system in half, test the midpoint, then split the remaining half again to narrow down the fault
Replace the most expensive component first
Test the last component changed and work backwards

explanation: Half-Split splits the system in half and tests the midpoint first. Based on the result, the remaining half is split again — eliminating half the possible causes with each test.

text: What is the key advantage of the Half-Split approach over the Linear approach?

options.text: It is simpler and easier to follow
It eliminates half the possible causes with each test, saving significant time on large systems
It doesn't require any documentation
It always finds the fault in exactly two tests

explanation: Half-Split is much faster for larger systems because each test eliminates half the remaining possible fault points, rapidly narrowing down the search area.

text: When is the Linear approach the better choice?

options.text: When the system is large and complex with many fault points
When the system is short and simple, or every component needs to be checked anyway
When you need to find the fault as fast as possible
When there are more than 10 possible fault points

explanation: Linear is best when the system is short and simple, or when you have no idea where the fault is and the system has few stages — making checking every component practical.

text: When is the Half-Split approach the better choice?

options.text: When the system has only a few components
When every component must be inspected regardless
When the system is large or complex with many possible fault points
When you already know which component has failed

explanation: Half-Split is most effective on large or complex systems with many possible fault points, where checking every component one by one would take too long.

text: A technician is troubleshooting a 'no power' fault. Using Half-Split, what would they test first?

options.text: Every component from the plug socket inward one by one
Whether the issue is the power supply or the cable, splitting the possible causes in half
The last component that was changed on the system
The most expensive component first

explanation: For a 'no power' fault, Half-Split would first check whether the issue is the power supply or the cable — splitting the possible causes in half rather than checking every component one by one.

text: What is a potential weakness of the Linear approach?

options.text: It is too complicated for simple faults
It can be slow if the fault is near the end of a long system
It skips components that might be faulty
It requires specialist tools at every stage

explanation: Linear is straightforward but can be slow if the problem happens to be near the end of the chain — you have to check every component before reaching it.

text: Does the need for documentation change depending on which approach you use?

options.text: Yes — Linear requires documentation but Half-Split does not
Yes — Half-Split requires documentation but Linear does not
No — good documentation is important regardless of which approach is used
No — documentation is only needed when the fault cannot be found

explanation: Good documentation supports both approaches. Without it, even an experienced technician has no real starting point on an unfamiliar system.

text: What factor should determine which approach you use?

options.text: The technician's personal preference
The size and complexity of the system
The time of day the fault occurred
The age of the equipment being tested

explanation: The right approach depends on the size and complexity of the system. Simple systems suit Linear; large complex systems suit Half-Split.

text: In a Half-Split test, a technician tests the midpoint of a system and finds everything is working correctly up to that point. What should they do next?

options.text: Start again from the beginning using the Linear approach
Split the remaining half of the system and test its midpoint
Replace all components in the second half
Document the fault as unsolvable

explanation: If the midpoint test passes, the fault must be in the second half. You then split that half and test its midpoint — continuing to narrow down until the fault is found.

text: Which statement best describes why Half-Split is faster than Linear on large systems?

options.text: It skips components that are unlikely to fail
Each test eliminates half the remaining possibilities, reducing the search area rapidly
It only tests the most recently changed components
It uses automated tools to test multiple components at once

explanation: Half-Split is faster because each test eliminates half the remaining possible fault points. On a large system this dramatically reduces the number of tests needed.
